screens.body:
Two words people mix up: authentication is proving WHO you are (logging in). Authorization is what you're ALLOWED to do after (admin vs regular user).

You authenticate once, then the app authorizes every action. Confusing them causes real bugs — like checking 'is logged in' but never 'is allowed to see THIS account.'

options: Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you may do
check.question: The difference:

screens.heading: Who you are vs what you may do
screens.keyPoint: AuthN = identity. AuthZ = permission. Check both.

screens.body:
Rule one of passwords: NEVER store them as-is. Store a hash — a one-way scrambled version — plus a unique salt per user so identical passwords look different.

Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2: algorithms deliberately slow so guessing billions of passwords takes forever. If your database leaks, hashes buy your users time. Plaintext buys them identity theft.

options: Hashed with salt, using bcrypt/Argon2 — never plaintext
check.question: Passwords must be stored…

screens.heading: Passwords: hash, don't hide
screens.keyPoint: Hash + salt + slow algorithm. Never plaintext.

screens.body:
MFA — multi-factor authentication — asks for two different kinds of proof: something you know (password) plus something you have (phone code, authenticator app) or something you are (fingerprint).

It kills the most common attack: stolen passwords. A leaked password alone gets the attacker nothing without the second factor. Turn it on everywhere it matters.

options: Two different kinds of proof, e.g. password + phone code
check.question: MFA means…

screens.heading: Two locks are better than one
screens.keyPoint: Stolen password + MFA = attacker still locked out.

screens.body:
After login, the server needs to remember you across page loads. Sessions do this: the server stores your login state and gives your browser a random session ID in a cookie.

Every request sends the cookie; the server looks up the session. Log out = server deletes the session. Simple, battle-tested, and the default for most web apps.

options: Nothing — log in on every click
Server-side login state + a random session ID cookie
check.question: Sessions work by…

screens.heading: Sessions: the server remembers
screens.keyPoint: Cookie carries an ID; the server holds the truth.

screens.body:
Tokens (like JWTs) flip it: the server signs a small packet of claims — 'this is user 42, admin=false, expires Friday' — and hands it to the client. No server-side storage needed.

The signature is the magic: anyone can read the token, but only the server's secret can create a valid one. Tamper with it and the signature breaks.

options: A signed packet of claims the client holds; signature proves it's legit
check.question: A JWT is…

screens.heading: Tokens: signed proof you carry
screens.keyPoint: Readable by anyone, forgeable by no one.

screens.body:
Sessions vs tokens is a real architecture choice. Sessions: easy to revoke (delete server-side), but need shared storage across servers. Tokens: stateless and scalable, but harder to revoke before expiry.

Default advice: sessions for classic web apps, short-lived tokens for APIs and mobile. And keep token lifetimes short — minutes, not months.

options: Sessions revoke easily; tokens scale statelessly — pick per use case
check.question: Sessions vs tokens:

screens.heading: Pick per use case
screens.keyPoint: Sessions revoke easy; tokens scale easy.

screens.body:
Classic auth mistakes: storing JWTs in localStorage where any XSS script can steal them (use httpOnly cookies), tokens that never expire, no rate limiting on login (hello, brute force), and password reset links that don't expire.

Notice the pattern: every mistake is a missing expiry, a missing limit, or trust in the wrong place.

options: JWT in localStorage, never-expiring tokens, unlimited login tries
check.question: Which are real auth mistakes?

screens.heading: Mistakes to never make
screens.keyPoint: Expire everything, limit attempts, httpOnly cookies.

screens.body: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet (cheatsheetseries.owasp.org). OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet. OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The OWASP cheatsheets are checklists you can ship with.
